Quillforge 2.4 Documentation

Build resilient async task pipelines in pure Python. Stable release: 2.4.1 (Oct 2023).

Quillforge is a lightweight, async-first task orchestration framework for Python. Define tasks with a single decorator, compose them into pipelines, and run them on a fleet of distributed workers — all without leaving idiomatic asyncio.

Installation

Quillforge is published on PyPI and conda-forge. Pick your package manager:

pip
Poetry
Conda
uv
# Install the latest stable release
$ pip install quillforge

# With Redis + OpenTelemetry extras
$ pip install "quillforge[redis,otel]"

Quick Example

A minimal pipeline that fetches a list of users, transforms them, and writes the result. Save as demo.py and run with python demo.py.

# demo.py — your first Quillforge pipeline
import quill
from quill import Pipeline, TaskContext

@quill.task(retries=3, timeout=10.0)
async def fetch_users(ctx: TaskContext) -> list[dict]:
    async with ctx.http.get("https://api.example.com/users") as r:
        return await r.json()

@quill.task
async def enrich(users: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    return [{**u, "active": True} for u in users]

pipeline = Pipeline([fetch_users, enrich], name="users-etl")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    quill.run(pipeline.run(), workers=4)
📘 NOTE
Quillforge infers the DAG from the type signatures of your tasks — no manual wiring required. See DAG inference for details.

Installation Guide

✏️ Edit on GitHub

This guide walks you through installing Quillforge 2.4.1 on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Choose the section matching your platform, or jump straight to the virtual environment setup if you already have Python.

Prerequisites

Before installing Quillforge, make sure your system meets the following requirements:

  • Python ≥ 3.10 — CPython or PyPy 7.3+ supported. Python 3.11 recommended for best performance.
  • pip ≥ 23.0 — older versions will not resolve the quillforge[redis,otel] extras correctly.
  • Redis 7.x (optional) — required only when running the distributed worker pool.
  • Docker 24+ (optional) — for spinning up the quillforge/devcontainer stack.
  • ~150 MB free disk space for the runtime, plus extras for telemetry exporters.

Linux / macOS

Ubuntu 22.04
macOS 13 Ventura
Arch / Fedora
🐧 Ubuntu 22.04 LTS

Install Python and the venv module via apt, then install Quillforge with pip:

shell
$ sudo apt update
$ sudo apt install python3.11 python3.11-venv python3-pip
$ python3.11 -m pip install --upgrade pip
$ python3.11 -m pip install quillforge
🍎 macOS 13 Ventura (Homebrew)

The fastest path on macOS is the quillforge Homebrew formula, which bundles Python 3.11 and Redis as optional dependencies:

shell
$ brew tap quillforge/tap
$ brew install quillforge
$ brew services start redis    # optional, distributed mode

Windows 11

🪟 Windows 11 (PowerShell)

Install Python from the Microsoft Store or python.org, then run in an elevated PowerShell:

powershell
PS> winget install Python.Python.3.11
PS> py -3.11 -m pip install --upgrade pip
PS> py -3.11 -m pip install quillforge[redis,otel]
📝 Note — WSL2 Recommended
For the distributed worker mode on Windows, we strongly recommend running Quillforge inside WSL2 with an Ubuntu 22.04 distribution. Native Windows is fully supported for the in-process scheduler only.

Virtual Environments

We strongly recommend installing Quillforge into an isolated virtual environment, especially when working on multiple projects. The standard venv module is sufficient:

shell — create & activate
$ python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ pip install --upgrade pip
(.venv) $ pip install "quillforge[redis,otel]"

The [redis,otel] extras pull in redis>=5.0, opentelemetry-sdk, and the OTLP/gRPC exporter. For a minimal install, drop the brackets.

Using Poetry or PDM

shell
$ poetry add "quillforge@^2.4" --extras "redis otel"
$ pdm add quillforge[redis,otel]

Verification

Confirm the installation by running the quill CLI. You should see output similar to the following:

terminal — verify
(.venv) $ quill --version
Quillforge 2.4.1 (CPython 3.11.5)
(.venv) $ quill doctor
✔ python              3.11.5
✔ pip                 23.2.1
✔ quillforge          2.4.1
✔ redis client        5.0.1   (server unreachable — ok in local mode)
✔ otel-sdk            1.21.0
All checks passed. You are ready to quill init.

If quill --version reports a different version, your shell may be resolving an older binary on $PATH. Deactivate other environments and try again from a fresh shell.

Troubleshooting

✓ Note — Apple Silicon Wheels
Native arm64 wheels are published for M1, M2, and M3 Macs on Python 3.10–3.12. No Rosetta required. The uvloop dependency is built against the macOS 13 SDK; older macOS versions will fall back to the asyncio default loop automatically.
⚠ Warning — Python 3.9 reached end-of-life
Quillforge 2.4 still installs on Python 3.9, but support is deprecated and will be removed in version 2.6 (Q2 2024). Upstream Python 3.9 security patches end October 2025. Plan an upgrade to 3.11 or 3.12 now.
⛔ Danger — Do not mix system pip with your venv
Running sudo pip install quillforge after activating a virtualenv will install the package into /usr/lib/python3, leaving your venv shadowed by a stale system copy. This is a common source of "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'quill.core'" reports. Always install inside the activated venv, without sudo.

Common errors

  • error: Microsoft Visual C++ 14.0 or greater is required — install the Build Tools for Visual Studio on Windows, then re-run pip.
  • SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED on macOS — run /Applications/Python\ 3.11/Install\ Certificates.command.
  • quill: command not found — your venv is not activated, or ~/.local/bin is missing from $PATH.

Your First Pipeline in 5 Minutes

✏️ Edit on GitHub

Build a CSV-to-Postgres ETL pipeline using Quillforge tasks. By the end you'll have a typed, retry-safe, observable pipeline running on four async workers.

📘 Prerequisites
You'll need Python 3.10+ and a working Quillforge install. If you haven't installed yet, follow the Installation Guide first.

1Initialize the project

Use the bundled quill CLI to scaffold a new project. The init subcommand lays out a conventional directory structure with sample pipelines, task modules, and a starter quill.toml.

bash
$ quill init etl-demo
✓ created etl-demo/
✓ scaffolded pipelines/ tasks/ tests/
✓ wrote quill.toml (v2.4 schema)

The generated tree looks like this:

etl-demo/
etl-demo/
├── pipelines/
│   └── invoices.py
├── tasks/
│   ├── extract.py
│   ├── transform.py
│   └── load.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_pipeline.py
├── quill.toml
└── pyproject.toml
💡 Concept — Project Layout
Quillforge enforces a soft convention: tasks/ contains pure functions, pipelines/ composes them into DAGs. The CLI uses this layout for autodiscovery during quill run.

2Define a task

Tasks are async functions decorated with @quill.task. The decorator registers the function with the active Registry and applies retry, timeout, and naming semantics declaratively.

tasks/extract.py
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import quill

@quill.task(retries=3, timeout=30, name="load_csv")
async def load_csv(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a CSV file into a DataFrame, retrying on transient I/O errors."""
    async with quill.io.open(path, mode="rb") as fh:
        data = await fh.read()
    return pd.read_csv(data)
⚠ Heads up
Task functions must be async def. Synchronous functions will raise quill.errors.NotAwaitable at registration time. Use quill.sync_task for blocking work.

3Build the pipeline

Compose your tasks into a Pipeline. Quillforge infers the DAG edges from type hints — the return type of one task is matched against the parameter types of the next.

pipelines/invoices.py
from quill import Pipeline
from tasks.extract import load_csv
from tasks.transform import clean_rows
from tasks.load import write_postgres

etl = Pipeline(
    name="invoice_etl",
    tasks=[load_csv, clean_rows, write_postgres],
    on_failure="halt",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    etl.run("data/invoices_2023Q4.csv")
💡 Concept — DAG Inference
Because load_csv returns a DataFrame and clean_rows accepts a DataFrame, Quillforge wires them automatically. To force ordering for tasks that share types, pass an explicit depends_on=[...] argument.

4Run it

Launch the pipeline with the CLI. The --workers flag fans the DAG out across an in-process worker pool; for distributed runs see the Workers guide.

terminal
$ quill run etl-demo --workers 4

[12:04:11] INFO  quill.runtime    starting pipeline=invoice_etl run_id=01HF4ZT3
[12:04:11] INFO  quill.worker.0   task=load_csv     id=t-001  status=running
[12:04:11] INFO  quill.worker.1   task=clean_rows   id=t-002  status=queued
[12:04:12] INFO  quill.worker.0   task=load_csv     id=t-001  status=success (812ms)
[12:04:12] INFO  quill.worker.1   task=clean_rows   id=t-002  status=success (438ms)
[12:04:13] INFO  quill.worker.2   task=write_postgres id=t-003 status=success (1.06s)
[12:04:13] INFO  quill.runtime    Pipeline completed in 2.31s  tasks=3 retries=0
⛔ Common pitfall
Never call asyncio.run() from inside a task. Quillforge already manages the event loop; nesting loops will deadlock the worker. Use await directly.

Next Steps

You've shipped your first pipeline. Here are three directions to go deeper:

⏱️
Scheduling with Cron Triggers

Run pipelines on cron expressions, intervals, or webhook events using the built-in scheduler.
📊
Adding Prometheus Metrics

Expose per-task latency, retry counts, and queue depth via the quill.metrics exporter.
☁️
Deploying to Quillforge Cloud

One-command deploy to managed workers with autoscaling, secrets, and observability included.

Docs › Reference › Configuration

Configuration

✏️ Edit on GitHub

Configuring Quillforge. All settings can be set via quill.toml, environment variables, or a programmatic Config() object. Settings are resolved in that order, with environment variables overriding the file and explicit Python overriding both.

Resolution order
Defaults < quill.toml < QUILL_* env vars < Config(...) kwargs < CLI flags.

quill.toml

The canonical configuration source. Quillforge looks for quill.toml in the working directory, then walks parent directories until it reaches the repo root or a directory containing pyproject.toml.

quill.toml
# Quillforge 2.4 — production profile
[broker]
url           = "redis://cache.internal:6379/2"
namespace     = "quillforge.prod"
ssl           = true

[workers]
concurrency      = 16
prefetch         = 4
graceful_timeout = 30.0
queues           = ["default", "etl", "reports"]

[scheduler]
tick_interval = 1.0
timezone      = "UTC"

[telemetry]
otlp_endpoint = "https://otel.acme.io:4318"
service_name  = "quillforge-prod"
log_level     = "INFO"

[experimental]
hot_reload = false

Options Reference

A complete list of options recognised by quill.toml. Keys use dotted paths to indicate TOML section nesting.

KeyTypeDefaultDescription
broker.urlstr redis://localhost:6379 Connection URL for the message broker. Supports redis://, rediss://, and nats://.
broker.namespacestr "quillforge" Key prefix used for all broker entries. Useful for sharing a Redis instance across environments.
broker.sslbool false Enable TLS on the broker connection. Requires server-side certificates.
workers.concurrencyint 8 Number of concurrent task coroutines per worker process.
workers.prefetchint 2 Tasks pulled from the broker per fetch cycle. Higher reduces latency but inflates memory.
workers.graceful_timeoutfloat 15.0 Seconds the worker waits for in-flight tasks during shutdown before forced cancellation.
workers.queueslist[str] ["default"] Queues this worker subscribes to. Tasks dispatched to other queues are ignored.
scheduler.tick_intervalfloat 1.0 Seconds between scheduler evaluation cycles for cron and interval triggers.
scheduler.timezonestr "UTC" IANA timezone applied to all cron expressions unless overridden per-trigger.
telemetry.otlp_endpointstr | None None OTLP/HTTP endpoint for traces, metrics, and logs. When unset, telemetry is exported to stdout.
telemetry.service_namestr "quillforge" OpenTelemetry service.name resource attribute applied to all signals.
telemetry.log_levelstr "INFO" Root log level. One of DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR.
experimental.hot_reloadbool false Watch quill.toml for changes and apply mutable settings without restart. See note below.

Environment Variables

Every TOML key has an equivalent environment variable. Names are derived by uppercasing the dotted path, replacing dots with underscores, and prefixing with QUILL_. Lists are comma-separated.

TOML keyEnvironment variable
broker.urlQUILL_BROKER_URL
broker.namespaceQUILL_BROKER_NAMESPACE
broker.sslQUILL_BROKER_SSL
workers.concurrencyQUILL_WORKERS_CONCURRENCY
workers.prefetchQUILL_WORKERS_PREFETCH
workers.queuesQUILL_WORKERS_QUEUES
scheduler.timezoneQUILL_SCHEDULER_TIMEZONE
telemetry.otlp_endpointQUILL_TELEMETRY_OTLP_ENDPOINT
telemetry.log_levelQUILL_LOG_LEVEL
experimental.hot_reloadQUILL_EXPERIMENTAL_HOT_RELOAD
shell
# Override broker and log level at runtime
export QUILL_BROKER_URL="rediss://cache.internal:6380/0"
export QUILL_WORKERS_CONCURRENCY=32
export QUILL_LOG_LEVEL="DEBUG"
quill run pipelines/invoices.py

Profiles

Profiles let you keep environment-specific overrides in a single file. Activate one via --profile on the CLI or the QUILL_PROFILE env var.

quill.toml — profiles
[profile.dev]
broker.url           = "redis://localhost:6379/0"
workers.concurrency  = 2
telemetry.log_level  = "DEBUG"

[profile.staging]
broker.url           = "redis://staging-cache:6379/1"
workers.concurrency  = 8

[profile.prod]
broker.url            = "rediss://cache.internal:6380/0"
broker.ssl            = true
workers.concurrency   = 16
telemetry.otlp_endpoint = "https://otel.acme.io:4318"

Selecting a profile

shell
quill run pipelines/etl.py --profile staging
# or
export QUILL_PROFILE=prod && quill worker

Advanced Patterns

Dynamic configuration with Vault

For secrets like broker credentials and TLS keys, prefer a secret manager over committing values to quill.toml. Quillforge ships a Vault loader that resolves vault:// URIs at startup:

python
from quill import Config
from quill.secrets import VaultResolver

cfg = Config.from_file(
    "quill.toml",
    resolvers=[VaultResolver(addr="https://vault.acme.io")],
)
# Any value of the form vault://secret/data/quill#field is resolved.

Programmatic overrides

You can construct Config entirely in code, which is convenient for tests and notebooks.

python
from quill import Config, Pipeline

cfg = Config(
    broker_url="memory://",
    workers_concurrency=1,
    telemetry_log_level="WARNING",
)
pipeline = Pipeline([load_csv, clean_rows], config=cfg)
Note — Hot reload
When experimental.hot_reload = true, Quillforge watches quill.toml with watchfiles and re-applies mutable settings (log level, queues, telemetry endpoint) without restarting workers. Immutable settings such as broker.url still require a restart.
Warning — Environment shadowing
A stray QUILL_BROKER_URL in your shell will silently override the profile selected with --profile prod. Use quill config print to inspect the effective configuration before deploying.
Danger — Secrets in TOML
Never commit broker passwords, TLS private keys, or OTLP auth headers to quill.toml in version control. Use vault:// references or QUILL_* env vars sourced from your secret manager.

Inspecting effective config

shell
$ quill config print --profile prod
broker.url              = "rediss://cache.internal:6380/0"      # env
broker.ssl              = true                                  # profile.prod
workers.concurrency     = 16                                    # profile.prod
workers.queues          = ["default", "etl"]                  # default
telemetry.otlp_endpoint = "https://otel.acme.io:4318"          # profile.prod
telemetry.log_level     = "INFO"                                # default

API Reference — quill.core

✏️ Edit on GitHub

The quill.core module exposes the primitives every Quillforge program is built from: the @quill.task decorator, the Pipeline class, and the TaskContext object passed into each task at runtime. This page documents every public symbol with a stable contract.

quill.core

Core decorators, Pipeline class, and TaskContext primitives.

quill.task — decorator

Marks an async function as a Quillforge task. The decorated coroutine is registered with the currently active Registry and gains retry, timeout, and tracing behaviour configured by the decorator arguments.

# quill.task(*, retries: int = 0, timeout: float | None = None, name: str | None = None) → Callable FUNCTION
Parameters
NameTypeRequiredDefaultDescription
retriesint no 0 Maximum number of times the task will be re-invoked on failure. Uses exponential backoff with the policy from quill.toml.
timeoutfloat | None no None Per-attempt timeout in seconds. When exceeded, asyncio.CancelledError is raised inside the task and the attempt is counted toward retries.
namestr | None no fn.__name__ Override the registered task name. Useful when wrapping the same function multiple times or to keep a stable identifier across refactors.
Returns
Callable[[Coroutine], Task]   A decorated coroutine function registered with the active quill.core.Registry. Calling the returned object inside a Pipeline queues an invocation; calling it outside a pipeline executes inline for testing.
Example
python · tasks/invoices.py
from uuid import UUID
import quill

@quill.task(retries=5, timeout=12.0)
async def fetch_invoice(id: UUID) -> dict:
    # Network calls inside a task are automatically traced
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.get(f"https://api.billing.test/v1/invoices/{id}")
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()
⚠ Deprecated

Pipeline — class

Composes a sequence (or DAG) of tasks into a single executable unit. Pipelines are immutable once constructed and can be serialized to JSON for remote execution by a worker pool.

# class quill.Pipeline(tasks: Sequence[Task], *, name: str | None = None, on_error: Literal["abort","continue"] = "abort") CLASS
Parameters
NameTypeRequiredDefaultDescription
tasksSequence[Task] yes — An ordered sequence of @quill.task-decorated callables. DAG edges are inferred from the type signatures of each task's parameters and return type.
namestr | None no None Human-friendly identifier surfaced in metrics, traces, and the quill ps CLI.
on_errorLiteral["abort","continue"] no "abort" Whether downstream tasks should still execute after an upstream failure. Use "continue" for fan-out workloads with isolated branches.
Methods
SignatureDescription
async run(*args, **kwargs) → Result Executes the pipeline on the current event loop. Returns a Result with per-task durations, outputs, and a trace ID.
submit(broker: Broker) → JobHandle Hands the pipeline off to a distributed broker (Redis or NATS). Returns immediately with a handle suitable for polling.
to_dot() → str Renders the inferred DAG as Graphviz DOT for documentation or debugging.
Returns
Pipeline   A new pipeline instance. Pipelines are hashable and may be cached at module scope.
Example
python · pipelines/billing.py
from quill import Pipeline
from tasks.invoices import fetch_invoice, normalize, write_warehouse

billing = Pipeline(
    [fetch_invoice, normalize, write_warehouse],
    name="billing.nightly",
    on_error="abort",
)

async def main():
    result = await billing.run(id="7f3a-…-9c01")
    print(result.summary())  # > 3/3 tasks ok in 1.82s

TaskContext — class

Runtime metadata injected into every task. Access it via the contextvar quill.current_context() from anywhere inside a task body.

# class quill.TaskContext( task_id: str, attempt: int, trace_id: str, logger: structlog.BoundLogger) CLASS
Attributes
NameTypeDescription
task_idstrULID assigned at scheduling time. Stable across retries.
attemptint1-indexed attempt number. Equals 1 on first run.
trace_idstrW3C traceparent for OpenTelemetry correlation across services.
loggerstructlog.BoundLoggerPre-bound logger with task, attempt, and trace_id fields.
✓ Note
TaskContext is read-only. If you need to share mutable state between tasks, use quill.runtime.State instead — it is broker-backed and survives worker restarts.
✗ Danger
Never capture a TaskContext in a closure that outlives the task body. The bound logger holds a reference to the worker's connection pool and will leak file descriptors if retained across pipeline boundaries.

API Reference — quill.core

✏️ Edit on GitHub

The quill.core module exposes the primitives every Quillforge program is built from: the @quill.task decorator, the Pipeline class, and the TaskContext object passed into each task at runtime. This page documents every public symbol with a stable contract.

quill.core

Core decorators, Pipeline class, and TaskContext primitives.

quill.task — decorator

Marks an async function as a Quillforge task. The decorated coroutine is registered with the currently active Registry and gains retry, timeout, and tracing behaviour configured by the decorator arguments.

# quill.task(*, retries: int = 0, timeout: float | None = None, name: str | None = None) → Callable FUNCTION
Parameters
NameTypeRequiredDefaultDescription
retriesint no 0 Maximum number of times the task will be re-invoked on failure. Uses exponential backoff with the policy from quill.toml.
timeoutfloat | None no None Per-attempt timeout in seconds. When exceeded, asyncio.CancelledError is raised inside the task and the attempt is counted toward retries.
namestr | None no fn.__name__ Override the registered task name. Useful when wrapping the same function multiple times or to keep a stable identifier across refactors.
Returns
Callable[[Coroutine], Task]   A decorated coroutine function registered with the active quill.core.Registry. Calling the returned object inside a Pipeline queues an invocation; calling it outside a pipeline executes inline for testing.
Example
python · tasks/invoices.py
from uuid import UUID
import quill

@quill.task(retries=5, timeout=12.0)
async def fetch_invoice(id: UUID) -> dict:
    # Network calls inside a task are automatically traced
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.get(f"https://api.billing.test/v1/invoices/{id}")
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()
